summary: Describes an IRIS registry schema for registered ENUM information. It extends IRIS query and result operations to provide the syntaxes and results that ENUM registries need. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A way to look up details of phone-number entries in the registry that connects numbers to internet addresses.

questions: what is the ereg1 registry type
how to search enum domains by e164 number
subtitle: An XML schema that lets IRIS servers answer questions about ENUM domains, their contacts, name servers and the parties around them.

tldr.problem: ENUM registries hold information about E.164 telephone numbers mapped into the DNS, along with registrants, contacts, name servers and operators, but IRIS had no query and result vocabulary for that data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4414 defines an IRIS registry type, identified as EREG1, with four queries, seven result types, two error codes and a list of entity classes for lookups, all described in an XML Schema.
tldr.outcome: A client can search ENUM domains by E.164 prefix, contact or name server and get back structured results, with privacy attributes that mark data as private or denied.

today: RFC 4414 is a Proposed Standard from February 2006, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the IRIS core protocol in RFC 3981.

sections.title: What This Registry Type Is
sections.content:
RFC 4414 describes a registry schema for the Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) that covers registries of ENUM data. The schema is written in XML Schema and derived from the IRIS core schema (RFC 3981). IRIS requires each registry schema to derive both its query and its result elements, so this document supplies them.

In this RFC the term ENUM means the fully qualified domain name that follows the conventions of ENUM as defined in RFC 3761. The registry type has the application service label EREG1, the abbreviated form of the URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:ereg1. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as in RFC 2119 to cover rules that the XML syntax alone cannot express.
sections.eli5: IRIS is a general way to look things up in registries. This document teaches it the special words it needs to look things up in the registry of phone-number domains.

sections.title: The Four Queries
sections.content:
The schema derives four queries.

  • <findEnumsByE164> finds ENUM domains by an E.164 number prefix given in <e164Prefix>. An optional <specificity> of less narrows the search to numbers with fewer digits, and more to numbers with more digits. It returns <enum> results.
  • <findEnumsByContact> finds ENUM domains by the contact: by <contactHandle> or a contact search field, optionally limited by the contact's <role>.
  • <findContacts> searches for contacts using one of the contact search fields.
  • <findEnumsByHost> finds the ENUM domains hosted by a name server, identified by host name, host handle, IPv4 address or IPv6 address.

The contact search group offers <commonName> and <organization> (exact match, or begins-with and ends-with), <eMail> (an exact address or any address in a domain via <inDomain>), and <city>, <region> and <postalCode> (exact match only). Non-ASCII domain names MUST be normalized as in RFC 3491. The contact queries also take optional <language> elements as hints that servers MAY use, for example to tailor normalization.
sections.eli5: You can ask the registry four kinds of questions: which domains match this phone number start, which belong to this contact, who are these contacts, and which domains does this name server host.

sections.title: The ENUM Result
sections.content:
The <enum> result represents one ENUM domain assignment. Its main children are <e164Number> (RECOMMENDED to use only spaces between digits, as in the RFC's example +1 703 555 1234), <enumHandle> (a registry-unique identifier), <nameServer> entries that refer to <host> results, a <registrant> that refers to a <contact>, and the contact group of role elements (billing, technical, administrative, legal, zone, abuse, security and other).

The <status> element holds status values: reserved, create, active, inactive, dispute, delete, transfer, update, renew, addPeriod, renewPeriod, autoRenewPeriod, transferPeriod, redemptionPeriod, restore and other. A status can carry an actor of registry or registrar, and a disposition of pending or prohibited. Any one status MUST NOT imply another: reserved only marks special handling, and the domain is shown as unregistrable by also giving create with disposition prohibited.

Other children give the registry and registrar (each a <registrationAuthority>), the validation entity, communication service providers, validation events, and timestamps such as initial delegation, last renewal, expiration and last verification.
sections.eli5: An ENUM result is like a card for one phone number's internet address. It lists the owner, the helper computers, the people to contact, and whether the number is active, locked or about to expire.

sections.title: The Supporting Results
sections.content:
Entities referred to from an <enum> result have their own result types.

  • <host>: a name server, with <hostHandle>, <hostName> (MUST conform to RFC 1123), IPv4 and IPv6 addresses (conforming to RFC 791 and RFC 3513) and host contacts.
  • <contact>: a person, organization, role or other party, with handle, name, e-mail, SIP URI, postal address, phone and fax numbers, a legal ID such as a tax number, and links to translated equivalents. A phone number starting with + MUST be an E.164 number.
  • <registrationAuthority>: an entity capable of registering domains, flagged as registry, registrar or other.
  • <validationEntity>: an entity that validates ENUM domains against E.164 registrations.
  • <communicationServiceProvider>: an entity providing ENUM domain service, with capabilities line, signal, data, voice or other.
  • <validationEvent>: a record of a validation, with a serial, a method identifier, the registrar and validation entity involved, and execution and expiration times.

Every result can also carry an <iris:seeAlso> entity reference for indirectly related data. Each entity reference names an authority, registryType, entityClass and entityName.
sections.eli5: The main card points to other cards: one for each helper computer, each person to contact, each company involved, and each check that was done on the number.

sections.title: Privacy Labels
sections.content:
Some values cannot be given out but must be shown as present, or must be flagged so clients do not pass them on. Several result elements therefore use special types, such as dateTimePrivacyType, stringPrivacyType, normalizedStringPrivacyType and tokenPrivacyType. They are nillable, so an element can be present with empty content. Timestamps MUST use the Z indicator for UTC.

If such an element is present without content, it MUST carry private (the content may never be published) or denied (policy does not allow it at the current access level), or both. If it is present with content, it MAY carry doNotRedistribute or specialAccess. These attributes SHOULD match the recipient's access level: an anonymous user would expect private or denied, while an authenticated high-access user would see doNotRedistribute or specialAccess.
sections.eli5: If a secret detail must stay hidden, the registry says there is something there but I cannot show you. If it shares a detail, it can add a note saying please do not pass this on.

sections.title: Entity Lookup and Error Codes
sections.content:
For IRIS's <lookupEntity> query this registry recognizes entity classes that each yield a particular result. All names are case insensitive. Clients SHOULD remove non-digit characters between the digits of an E.164 number and servers MUST ignore them, so +1 703 555 1234 is read as +17035551234.

Two generic error codes are derived. Servers MAY return <searchTooWide> when a query must be narrowed to give a result set the operator's policy accepts. Servers MAY return <languageNotSupported> when a client passes a language the server does not support; it lists each one in <unsupportedLanguage> children, and when the server returns this error it MUST give the unsupported languages from the query.
sections.eli5: You can ask for a thing by its name, number or ID, and the registry knows what kind of answer to give. If your question matches too many things, or uses a language it does not know, it can say so.

sections.title: Transport, Registrations and Security
sections.content:
The registry type follows IRIS-BEEP (RFC 3983) for transport. It uses the default message pattern and only the basic Transport Layer Security server authentication method. The application service label MUST be EREG1.

IANA registrations are given for the XML schema URN urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:ereg1, the namespace URN urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:ereg1, the S-NAPTR application service tag EREG1, and the BEEP profile URI http://iana.org/beep/iris1/ereg1.

For internationalization, contact data may contain virtually any Unicode character, so clients should use the <language> elements and servers should use them to improve normalization and search. The RFC says it lays out no new security considerations beyond those of IRIS in RFC 3981.
sections.eli5: This part says how the questions travel safely to the registry, which names get reserved for this kind of registry, and that it adds no new safety rules beyond the ones IRIS already has.
